AI-assisted review of statistical products

From a single prompt to an agent that checks the numbers

Valentin Klotzbücher · DKF Basel

2026-11-22

Should journals ban AI in peer review?

Fourteen known errors inserted into reports of randomised trials; every review scored against the same answer key:

  • Human peer reviewers: 27% of the major errors
  • Each of 15 language models, text only: 53–96%
  • On 58 trials published in 2026: 58–99%
  • the models also flagged 14–29% of the error types on unmodified reports

“For clinical trials, I’d even call human-only review dangerous.”

Ruslan Rust, last author, on X

Brian et al., medRxiv, 28 October 2026, not peer reviewed. Humans: 2004 study, 607 reviewers. Two LLM judges. Fig. 1b, CC BY 4.0.

[0:00–1:15] This week’s debate: should journals ban AI in peer review? A new preprint repeated the classic BMJ experiment: errors inserted into trial reports, one answer key. Human reviewers in 2004 found about a quarter of the major errors; every one of 15 current models, reading only the text, found more, the best almost all. Caveats: a preprint, a historical human comparison, LLM judges, and models that also flag concerns on clean reports. The last author’s conclusion: for clinical trials, human-only review is dangerous. Today: how we put this to work on our own statistical products, before they go out.

The job: the consistency review

Every DKF statistical product gets a second statistician’s review before it goes out: sample size estimations, protocol statistics sections, analysis plans, reports, manuscripts.

The review ends in a form:

  • Decision: minor or major changes to text or code; clarification needed
  • General comments, major and minor issues
  • Answers to the questions in the assignment

Where errors hide

Text what the PDF says: a wrong formula, a missing estimand component
Code what only the source shows: a one-sided test, a value that never reaches the text
Computation what the code actually computes: a stale number, a figure built on noise

[1:15–2:15] The second statistician reads the rendered document against its Quarto source and the protocol or SAP. Keep the three levels in mind; they come back with the product on the next slide. A reader finds the first, a careful reader of the code the second, and only someone who runs things finds the third.

The product: a sample size estimation

DEMO-TKA (invented)

App-guided home exercise versus supervised physiotherapy after knee replacement. Six-minute walk distance at 6 months; ANCOVA; power by simulation. Two pages of Quarto and R.

It concludes

  • 55 evaluable per group, estimated power 81.5%
  • 66 randomised per group, 132 in total

Page 2 of the PDF, excerpt. Every approach gets this PDF and its Quarto source, nothing else.

It reads like a finished SSE. We planted six errors in it.

[2:15–3:15] This is the product for the rest of the talk: a two-page sample size estimation we wrote for an invented trial. It looks like the ones we sign off: planning values with their sources, a simulation, a power curve, a sample size, a dropout allowance. Every approach gets the same two files, the PDF and its Quarto source. And we planted six errors in it, of the kind we see in real products, with invented numbers.

Six planted issues, two at each level

Level Planted issue
Text dropout inflation: 55 × 1.2 instead of 55 / 0.8
Text estimand without intercurrent events
Code the simulation tests one-sided; the text says two-sided
Code the baseline correlation exists only in the code
Computation Figure 1 is a running maximum; n chosen on noise
Computation typed t-test number (94) is not what the code computes (105)

The design of the trial-report benchmark (inserted errors, one answer key), extended to code and computation.

Two a reader can see, two only the source shows, two that need a calculation or a re-run.

[3:15–4:00] Two at each of the three levels. Text: the dropout allowance multiplies where it should divide, and the estimand names no intercurrent events. Code: the simulation tests one-sided although the text says two-sided, and the correlation the ANCOVA gain depends on exists only in the code. Computation: the figure is a running maximum, and one typed number is not what the code computes. It is the design of the benchmark on the first slide, extended to code and computation.

One figure, two stories

The SSE reports 81.5% at 55 per group. The true power there is 75% with the code’s one-sided test and 64% with the two-sided test the text states. The planning values support 80 evaluable per group: 200 randomised, not 132.

[4:00–5:15] What the six errors add up to. Wine: what the SSE plotted, a running maximum of noisy estimates. Grey circles: what was actually simulated where it differs. Mint: the power of the test the text promises. The design as written has about 62% power. No amount of reading gets you these numbers; you have to run something.

A reader: chat, a review skill in chat, or one call

.qmd source rendered PDF reviewer's questions
↓
one model reads both
↓
review
  • Chat: paste both files and ask
  • A review skill in chat: the document check, the agent’s first stage; it recomputes printed numbers, never runs the product’s code
  • Our prototype: one scripted call with a reviewer’s checklist; minutes, under $1.50

What a reader cannot do

  • run the product’s code
  • re-run the simulation behind a figure
  • check a number that only the code computes

“Every error tested here is visible in the text, whereas errors in data handling or analysis code […] are not.” Brian et al. 2026

Reading is a strong start. Checking needs the code.

[5:15–6:30] The first approach is a reader. In a chat you paste the PDF and the source and ask for a consistency review. A review skill in chat goes one step further: the document check is the agent’s first stage, packaged as a skill for a normal chat. Same checklist as the agent, and it recomputes printed numbers with its own scripts, but it never runs the product’s code. Our earlier prototype did the reading as one scripted call: a reviewer’s checklist as the prompt, minutes and under a dollar fifty. Readers read attentively: on trial reports a single call beat the human reviewers. But they stop at the print. The preprint’s authors say so themselves: their errors were all visible in the text. Anything a reader says about a number only the code computes is a guess about that number. (A chat that runs the product’s code is no longer only a reader; that comes back at the scoreboard.)

What changed: an agent with skills

One call
PDF + source
↓
model
↓
review

Agent with skills
job folder + skill
↓
model⇄read files · run R · search
↓
review + record of every check
decides its next step; runs the code
  • Agent: a general model that uses tools in a loop and chooses its own next step (here Claude Code; other coding agents work similarly)
  • Skill: a folder of plain-text instructions, references and scripts that the agent loads when a task matches

The general part does the work. The skill holds what we know about reviewing.

[6:30–7:30] The difference that matters for statisticians is the right-hand column: the agent can run the code. It reads the source, runs it, recomputes the numbers and checks them against the text. The skill is text: what to check and how to report it, not how to talk to an API.

The DKF review skills

Document
versions; protocol, SAP and registry; printed numbers and their arithmetic; design and estimand
Code and data
code against text; Quarto and R mechanics; runs the code; 12 clinical modules
Statements
what the product claims, one row each, and whether it holds
Challenge
a fresh agent tests every finding, in both directions
Verdict
a fresh agent writes the result and answers the assignment
Audit
depth "full": coverage and re-runs, mechanically
Form
the DKF consistency review, Decision boxes computed

Modules fire by product: for an SSE, sample size, simulation, RCT and missing data. Depth: quick (no challenge), standard, full (with audit).

Adapted from Joseph Francis’s research_skills (MIT licence), written for economics papers with replication packages; the clinical modules, the data rules and the form are ours.

[7:30–8:30] Five stages and two optional ones. The fresh agents matter: the challenge and the verdict are written by agents that did not produce the findings, so they have no stake in them. The modules fire depending on the product; for an SSE, sample size, simulation, RCT and a light missing-data check. We did not start from nothing: in October the author of Reviewer 2, a review pipeline for research papers, released his review skills under an MIT licence, and ours are adapted from them.

Scored against the answer key: an issue counts when the review names the problem and where it is, as a finding or a lead. Same PDF and source for every run; · not yet run. Time: model time. Cost: at API list prices; the agent runs were on a subscription. We wrote the skills and this SSE in the same week: the demo shows the checklist at work, not a blind test.

The agent found all six, and showed what each one costs in participants.

At quick depth: all six in 34 minutes, start to finished form, for about $10.

[8:30–9:45] Two agent runs here, a third in the backup; all six planted issues found every time, two at each level, each one sized. At standard depth: 3.4 hours of model time, 35 hours on the clock with two waits for usage limits. So we cut the skills down to size: at quick depth the same review took 34 minutes and about $10, with a form a third the length. From the first run: at the code’s correlation the stated test needs 80 evaluable per group, not 55; the first-crossing rule picks a sample size below 80% true power in 39% of runs. It added three points a reviewer would accept: where the SD and the loss come from, missing at random, clustering by physiotherapist.

(Before the talk: fill the two chat rows from demo/runs/scoreboard.csv; its sized column says how many issues each review gave in participants or power, 5 of 5 for the agent runs. If the readers find the issues but cannot size them, close with: the question is not which model is smarter, but which approach can run the code. If the document check finds and sizes most of them: the checklist carries most of the value, and running the code adds the simulation and the exact N. If a chat ran the product’s code: a chat with a code tool is a small agent, and its row shows it.)

(If asked whether the skills were tuned to the demo: we wrote both in the same week, and the skills, finished the day before the SSE, already describe the dropout rule and, from a trial on a real SSE, the noisy first crossing. So this shows the checklist at work; a blind test needs a case written by someone else, which is the proposal at the end.)

What the reviewer gets

  • the DKF form, with the Decision boxes computed from the issues
  • each issue with where it is (page, file and line), its numbers and a fix
  • answers to the questions in the assignment
  • what the review could not check, and why
  • REVIEW comments in a copy of the .qmd
  • behind it, the script and log for every number

The quick run’s form, excerpt: 3 major and 3 minor issues, about 1,100 words.

[9:45–10:30] The deliverable is a draft of the form the second statistician fills in anyway. Here every Decision box is ticked, and the general comments lead with the sample size the document does not establish. They read it, check what they doubt, edit, and sign.

One finding, traced: 80 per group, not 79

The review says

“At a correlation of 0.5 the planned ANCOVA needs 80 evaluable and 100 randomised participants per group (200 in total) under the stated two-sided test”

Its evidence

  • exact power with a random baseline: 79.83% at 79, 80.34% at 80 (work/logs/ss_exact_ancova.log)
  • rebuilt by the challenge agent (work/challenge/s1_N_exact.log)
  • the SSE’s own simulation, made two-sided, 10,000 trials per point: 80% crossed at 78.5 and 79.2 (work/challenge/s5_N_sim.log)

Our answer key said 79

  • it treated the baseline as fixed; the SSE draws it at random
  • the chance baseline difference between the arms costs about half a participant per group
  • recomputed with a random baseline: 79.8% at 79, 80.3% at 80

The agent was right; we corrected the key.

From the standard run of 31 October 2026.

[10:30–11:30] One finding, followed to its evidence. The review says 80 per group. Behind that sentence is the log of an exact power calculation, the same calculation rebuilt by the challenge agent, which did not write the finding, and the SSE’s own simulation made two-sided with 10,000 trials per point. Our answer key said 79: we had treated the baseline as fixed, and the SSE draws it at random. The agent was right, and we corrected the key. That is what checkable means: you can disagree with the review and settle it by opening a log.

Safe by default

Data mode The agent reads What the review can establish
none (default) documents and code everything that needs no patient data: sample size and simulation code, arithmetic on printed numbers, code against text
synthetic + dummy data, built from the code or from a codebook made locally that the code runs and does what the text says; never a printed result
shared + patient-level data, only with a recorded clearance reproduction of printed results
  • a scan stops the run when data sits where the mode does not allow it
  • no zero-data-retention agreement yet: what is sent is kept under the provider’s terms

No patient data unless someone decided otherwise before the run, and recorded it.

[11:30–12:15] What makes this usable in a CTU: the data mode is set before the run. The default is none: documents and code only, which is all an SSE needs. Synthetic data lets the code run without patient data. Shared needs a recorded clearance. A scan stops the run when data sits where the mode does not allow it. And plainly: we have no zero-data-retention agreement yet, so what is sent is kept under the provider’s terms.

Where to start

  1. Chat, on non-sensitive material. Explain unfamiliar code, check a paragraph against its table, draft questions for a SAP.
  2. A review skill in chat, on a non-sensitive document. Upload the document check as a skill: you read what the agent is told to do, and get tables and a check log, not free text.
  3. An agent with review skills for a full pre-review. It runs the code, recomputes and leaves a record; no patient data by default.
  4. A few test cases with known answers. Plant errors in your own kind of document and see which approach finds them.

Errors found while they are still cheap to fix: before the protocol, not after the trial.

[12:15–13:15] What you can do on Monday. Each step is useful on its own; start with the first and move on as your data rules allow. The skill in chat is the agent’s first stage on its own: the easiest way to see what the agents do before running one. The aim is better research: errors found while they are still cheap to fix.

What carries over

The biggest lesson that can be read from 70 years of AI research is that general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, and by a large margin.

Rich Sutton, The Bitter Lesson, 13 March 2019

Review tools turn over in months. Invest in what carries over:

  1. Test cases with known answers: which tool works for us, and when a new one works better
  2. Standards for the review: traceable numbers, a status for every check, the form
  3. Rules for data: what may be sent where, decided before the run
  4. The statistician who signs: the output is a draft

Proposal: a shared set of planted-issue SSEs and SAPs across Swiss CTUs.

[13:15–14:30] Sutton wrote about AI research, but the lesson fits our small story: hand-built machinery keeps losing to general methods that use more computation. Our prototype went that way. The author of Reviewer 2 retired his pipeline in October: “I decided it was obsolete”. Our skills will turn over too; they are plain text, cheap to change. So invest in what carries over. Test cases are the most useful: we can each write two or three, and every new tool gets scored on the same set. That is something the SCTO platforms could host. And the good news: every new model makes the same checklist more powerful.

Each step was useful; the last one can finally run the code.

What we tried, in order. Every step was useful to us, and each model generation read more carefully than the last. The costs are from our own run logs.

What we learned building the prototype

What took the effort

  • background jobs, polling and streaming
  • uploading PDFs; two Python SDKs driven from R
  • proving the model read the source to the end
  • token counts and cost estimates

What carried over

  • the checklist: what a second statistician checks
  • the DKF form as the output
  • a record of every run

Meanwhile, six frontier models came out in ten months: Claude Opus 4, 4.7, 5; GPT-5 Pro, 5.2 Pro, 5.5 Pro.

The models improve every few months, and what we know about reviewing carries over.

Most of our effort went into code that talks to one provider’s interface at one point in time: background jobs, uploads, two SDKs. (One example: our May code set temperature to zero; by August current models rejected that setting outright.) What carried over to every new model was the knowledge of what to check and the form we want back.

Others built review pipelines; we built on open skills

Reviewer 2 (isitcredible.com)
More than 30 chained model calls: aggressive prompting, then a verification cascade to remove what the aggression invents. 15–45 minutes and a few dollars per paper.
Refine (refine.ink)
Referee-style reports on research papers, checking logic, clarity and internal consistency. About $50 per paper.

In October, Reviewer 2’s author released “the three skills that I use to begin my reviews, now freely available for anyone to use”. Our DKF skills build on them.

Joseph Francis on X, 26 October 2026; github.com/isitcredible/research_skills (MIT); github.com/isitcredible/reviewer2

Review tools turn over in months: Reviewer 2’s author retired his pipeline in October (“I decided it was obsolete”), and Claude Science now has a built-in reviewer that checks claims against what actually ran.

Dedicated review pipelines and services appeared, and some are very good. We didn’t build one. Instead we built on the open skills that Reviewer 2’s author released this October: free, readable, and easy to adapt to our products and our form.

How well one call reads

  • Trial reports: every one of 15 models, reading only the text, found more of the inserted major errors than the human reviewers: 53–96% against 27% (Brian et al. 2026)
  • Our Unjournal comparison: one call per paper found 80% of the issues the expert evaluators agreed on, across 12 economics and policy papers

LLM versus human evaluations: llm-uj-research-eval.netlify.app

Both studies say a single call reads attentively: on trial reports it beats human reviewers, on economics papers it finds most of what experts agree on. The preprint’s authors add that the next gains need access to code, protocols and registry entries.

Checkable by design

  • every number traced to a file and line, or to a script and its log
  • coverage as a list: every table, figure and code chunk
  • a status for every check: settled, untested, unverifiable, not checked here
  • the burden is on the product: a planning value with no source is a finding
  • a stage is done only when its check script passes

The output can be checked: nothing is asserted without a trace.

The prototype’s prompt (abridged)

You are a senior biostatistics reviewer performing pre-human quality review
for a clinical research document. Review the available material: PDF, Quarto
source, or both.

Check:
1. Statistical validity: design, estimand, endpoint, model, assumptions,
   missing data, multiplicity, sensitivities.
2. Numerical consistency: Ns, denominators, percentages, p-values, CIs,
   tables, figures, and text.
3. Code/reproducibility: filters, joins, grouping, NA handling, seeds,
   hard-coded paths, package/version fragility.
4. Interpretation: overclaiming, unsupported causal language.

Anchor each issue to a page, section, table, figure, chunk label, or code
fragment. Mark what is verified vs suspected.
Output: Decision · General Comments · Major Issues · Minor Issues · Answers

Inside a review job

jobs/2026-11_DEMO-TKA/
├── 00_ASSIGNMENT.md     product type, questions, data mode, depth, clearances
├── 00_INTAKE.md         what was received; requests for the operator
├── PROGRESS.md          done, running, next: a stopped run resumes here
├── 01_product/          the .qmd and the rendered PDF
├── 02_governing/        protocol, SAP, registry entry
├── review/              stage reports, extracts, intake scan
├── analysis/            consistency matrix, spec map, statement ledger, results
├── work/                scripts and logs of every re-run
├── SYNTHESIS.md         the verdict
├── ISSUES.md            the issue ledger the form is built from
└── CONSISTENCY_REVIEW.html   the draft form

Job folders are never committed. A stage counts as done only when its check script passes.

Running on a subscription

  • The skills run inside Claude Code, so a review counts against a subscription’s usage limits rather than API credits, as long as no API key is set in the environment (check /status)
  • The demo review at standard depth: about 15 agents, 3.4 hours of model time, about $72 at API list prices, two waits for the 5-hour limit
  • At depth quick (skills 0.2): 3 agents, 34 minutes start to finished form, about $10 at API list prices
  • Depth quick for routine SSEs; a stopped run resumes from its progress file
  • Data terms depend on the plan: on personal plans, model training on your sessions is a privacy setting; commercial plans and the API are not covered by it

As written Correct
Test in the simulation one-sided 5% two-sided 5%
Power at 55 per group 81.5% (200 trials, running max) 64% (exact 64.2%; 64.3% in 20,000 trials)
Evaluable per group for 80% 55 80
Dropout inflation 55 × 1.2 = 66 80 / 0.8 = 100
Randomised in total 132 200
Unadjusted t-test, per group 94 (typed) 105
Baseline correlation 0.5, code only stated and sourced

All values from demo/answer-key.R; exact power with the baseline random, as the SSE simulates it.
